author: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate

slides.1: Adaptation is the half of climate action nobody puts on a poster. Yet the rain here disappears for months, and then one storm delivers an entire year of it in forty-eight hours.
slides.2: Everyone hears Climate Action and thinks of cutting carbon. Read the goal properly and half of it is about survival: drains that cope, homes that stand, and a supply that holds.
slides.3: We are officially a water-poor island, which sounds absurd in a place this wet. The mountains are simply too steep, so the rain reaches the sea long before it reaches a reservoir.
slides.4: Fewer typhoons sounds like good news until you remember who refills our reservoirs. In the last drought the storage ran out completely, rice fields cracked open, and the semiconductor plants nearly stopped.
slides.5: Then the island floods instead. A single storm can deliver a year's rainfall in two days, and drains designed for a calmer century give up, turning shopping streets into muddy rivers.
slides.6: Two questions follow, and neither has a comfortable answer. Can drainage designed for the last century survive this climate? And can we hold floodwater long enough to drink it in the dry season?
slides.7: Taiwan has not been standing still. The Forward-looking Water Grid has linked the pipelines of neighbouring cities, so when Kaohsiung runs short, spare supply can be pumped across from Tainan instead.
slides.8: Taipei and Taichung are being rebuilt as sponge cities. Solid concrete is giving way to permeable paving, and the parks are sunk below street level so that a downpour fills them first.
slides.9: Farming has changed as well. A computer now controls the drip irrigation, giving each rice plant exactly the water it needs and nothing more, which saves millions of tons every season.
slides.10: This is where STEM earns its place. Engineers have fitted sensors inside the water mains, and the data they stream lets a computer pinpoint a buried leak within minutes instead of months.
slides.11: We are also making water now. Factory wastewater is cleaned until it can go back into the production line, and coastal plants can pull the salt out of seawater in an emergency.
slides.12: In the hills, the same idea works against landslides. Rather than pouring another cement wall, engineers hold the slope with rock and local plants, so the mud never reaches our reservoirs.
slides.13: None of this is cheap, and the bill lands on somebody. Recycling plants and deep pipes cost billions of dollars, so the fair question is how we pay without breaking ordinary families.
slides.14: There is a fairness problem hidden inside this. The wealthy technology cities receive the new systems first, while farming villages are the first to have their water cut during a drought.
slides.15: Other island nations face exactly these problems, and what we have learned could genuinely help them. Politics keeps Taiwan out of the climate summits, so the knowledge must travel by other routes.
slides.16: Finally, somebody has to check the work. A sponge park that nobody maintains is only landscaping, so citizens should be asking for the inspection data on our dams and drains every year.
slides.17: So where does that leave us? Sponge cities, a national water grid and stubborn engineering cannot stop the storms, but they can leave us properly ready for the next one.
slides.18: Why should this matter to you? Because adaptation is still an unsolved design problem. Study earth science, computing or engineering, and meanwhile treat every drop you save at home as part of the answer.
slides.19: None of this should leave you feeling powerless. Human ingenuity and natural systems can work together rather than against each other, and Taiwan has the skill and the nerve to prove it.
slides.20: So will you help build an island that can absorb whatever the next decade sends? The weather is not waiting for our decision, and Taiwan has already started adapting.
